blocks.text: Why the apparent excitement and use of an exclamation point? What is the Mastery Series you ask? While some of you may remember this from years ago, trust that this new, reimagined iteration is well worth the revisit. With a new scientific understanding emerging and the apparent awakening of the medical community to the benefits of strength training, we began to look inside our own systems and realized that there was an opportunity to get better. To lean even harder into what the research is confirming and to what thousands of our own real world case studies have revealed. An opportunity for a sort of kaizen as we refer to it around here.

But for this improvement to be fully realized, a new level of attentiveness and involvement is required. From everyone in the studio; instructors and trainees alike. And while we’ve been doing essentially the same thing for almost 20 years, and don’t plan on changing, recent information has suggested we narrow our focus. The MSF Mastery Series is an attempt to simplify the understanding of productive strength training.

And truer words have never been spoken when you consider that ‘simple’ in this case does not indicate ‘easy’. In fact, many of you should find the training more difficult or challenging. But it is in this difficulty that true, long term physiological benefits are achieved. Both physical and mental. Learning to accept or cope with a difficult endeavor can not only help you through a productive set of exercise but can be an invaluable life skill that is adaptable to almost any situation. So think of this new approach as an intensive study on human behavior. Your behavior! Let’s see if by fully embracing this new challenge, we can actually optimize our strength training experience and better yet, our lives.
So with the gauntlet firmly in place, let’s introduce our first topic of interest.
Posture.
Yes, your posture.

Now, we've been setting your posture on every exercise of every workout you’ve ever performed with us. But some of you haven’t held your posture as if your lives depended on it. So when we instruct you to “maintain your posture” we mean it! Literally fight with every ounce of awareness and strength to NOT move. Again, simple, but not easy. If you are not properly positioned on an exercise or if that positioning changes, there is a weakening of the structure and a decrease or shifting in motor unit recruitment (MUR). This is just a fancy way of indicating which and how many muscle fibers are contributing or targeted. And losing our posture diminishes the effectiveness of the exercise.

Your ‘posture’ as we refer to it almost always includes your head but also often includes your torso, ribcage, and spine. We want to keep those components rigidly still. If we shift or wiggle, we might as well end the set because everything’s changed. We’re now doing a different exercise, targeting different motor units (i.e. muscles). Not to mention that when we lose our posture we lose power/leverage and even worse, we introduce a potential safety issue.

So let’s just see what changes, what feels different, when we pay attention to our posture that our instructor establishes and we actually work to maintain that posture! For the entire duration of the exercise. Not just at the onset. So just like before, let’s push ourselves harder than we’ve ever pushed but this time let’s also work to hold our posture. And most importantly, let’s get excited about the potential for new progress when we commit to this all important attribute.
Be strong,
Jeff

The next topic in our MSF Mastery Series is Pace. But being that this is a cumulative series, we must not forget our first topic, Posture. Everything starts with Posture and this needs to be our foundation as we add new concepts to master.

Pace is probably more synonymous with our protocol than any other descriptor that comes to mind. In fact if you asked the entire MSF family to describe our training in one sentence, there’s a good chance that sentence would include the words “moving slowly,” or something to that effect. And while they’re technically not wrong, there’s a good chance that they’re missing a critical component of this tenet.
Let’s look into why that might be and more importantly why that matters.

When new trainees are first introduced to our style of training at MSF, there is a preoccupation with slowing down movement. This is because our bodies are inherently intensity adverse and as a protective measure will speed up movement to make the task easier. It's as if we are programmed to instinctively find the path of least resistance. So if we are to override this mechanism, we need to hyperfixate on slowing down our speed.

But what our focus should really be on is maintaining a CONSISTENT pace. So while moving slowly is important, it is better described as moving smoothly. To not change speeds. And as a reminder, that speed can be between 6 to 10 seconds in each direction, as long as the concentric and eccentric are the same.

As an aside, there are benefits to moving closer to the 6 seconds than the 10, but that will depend on the individual and the exercise. Just know that if your trainer is having you speed up, just speed up SLIGHTLY. It will probably be more than enough, but it matters. We are trying to optimize your training and your results. And as long as we are exaggerating our control of the lower turnaround, it’s almost impossible to go too fast (let your trainer guide you).

What’s more important than the actual speed however, is the ability to intently focus on maintaining ONE CONTINUOUS PACE. And here’s where the hidden meaning to this approach comes into play. The sort of “silver bullet” for productive resistance training.

While we are encouraged to maintain our pace, we cannot and should not expect our EFFORT to remain constant. In other words, if we are to maintain a given pace in an activity with increasing fatigue, our effort needs to voluntarily increase to counter that fatigue. This is how stimulative mechanical tension is created. This is what makes resistance training effective.

In this way, Pace governs effort. As you sense your movement bogging down, push harder to keep your pace. There’s a point in the set where you will notice that you are no longer moving slowly because we’re supposed to move slowly. You’re moving slowly because you are beginning to fatigue and have not yet begun to voluntarily push harder. It’s not enough to move slowly until we can no longer move slowly or because we can no longer tolerate the discomfort. And while we’re on the topic of discomfort, by focusing instead on our pace, it may help us get beyond these adverse feelings that often lead to us ending our sets prematurely.

So don’t think slow…think smooth and continuous. Begin to become more aware of when you are bogging down. You’ll be the first to know. More importantly, let that be your cue to shift gears and begin pushing harder. Focus on keeping your pace. And by all means, lean on your trainer for help, that’s what we’re here for!

Before we discuss this month’s topic for the MSF Mastery Series, let’s remind ourselves that we should continue to build upon our understanding of the previous two installments, Posture and Pace. No amount of strength training will matter without first establishing a rigid, unwavering Posture and combining it with a smooth and continuous Pace. As always, your trainer will reinforce these concepts…just make sure you are attentive to their instruction and doing everything in your power to implement.
Our current installment of Mastery will focus on a topic we call Path.

In this context, Path refers to the plane of motion, or movement pattern that is performed during an exercise. More specifically, we are referring to the actual act of moving the arms, legs, torso, or head on a given machine and the resulting path that they follow. Because the body automatically detects and recruits the muscles with the best leverage at a given joint angle, the Path we use will determine which muscle fibers are targeted. This is known as neuromechanical matching and it really matters when attempting to create a stimulative effect.

Now on certain machines, the Path may not be able to be varied much…and that’s a good thing. The more locked in or restrained we are, the more we are forced to maintain a consistent path, creating a more consistent loading of the muscles we are intending to target. For those that have used the lumbar or lower back machine, this is a good example of keeping a consistent path. It’s almost impossible to vary the path of the movement. This ensures a better chance that an exercise will be stimulative (i.e. effective) because we are not shifting the effort or tension around. Tension needs to remain on the same muscle fibers throughout an exercise in order to reach a high enough threshold. And “high enough” for our purposes would be more tension than those muscle fibers have previously experienced.

But for many exercises, especially upper body movements, the limb’s Path will be a determining factor in the leverage that a particular muscle fiber has at a given joint position. We do not want to shift that leverage around as that will only act to unload muscle fibers that we are intending to keep loaded.

Let's consider the compound row as an example. If we begin a set by carrying the elbows out wide relative to the torso (abducted) and then begin to tuck the elbows closer to the torso as we fatigue (adduct), we are essentially performing a different exercise. And by changing the movement pattern, there’s a good chance that we are not fully stimulating any muscle fibers, essentially missing out on any benefit. Even though we will still feel as though we have done something we cannot fool our physiology.

This is one of the more challenging aspects of proper training for a newer trainee to overcome. Instinctively our bodies will attempt to find the path of least resistance. We find ourselves operating under the premise of the assumed objective…to keep the machine moving as long as possible. In order to do this, we need to unload what is fatiguing or uncomfortable and transfer the effort to other muscles.

In order for resistance training to be effective, we need to learn to overcome this instinctive measure to shift and be consistent with our Path of execution. When the trainer instructs “elbows out” we need to keep our elbows out, and maintain that same path. This is a simple premise but it is not easy to implement. But this is the “practice” or challenge of the workout that will keep us engaged for a lifetime. And more importantly, this challenge to Master of proper resistance training will keep us progressing toward a more optimized human experience!

For this next installment of the MSF Mastery Series, we’re going to highlight the 4th and final “P” of the Four P’s of strength training, Purpose. Now you could conceivably master the first three P’s, Posture, Pace, and Path, in a matter of a handful of workouts. The MSF Continuous Tension protocol, instruction, and equipment are designed to facilitate this learning curve. This last “P” however…could take a lifetime of work. And this lifetime of work is what will produce the long term results we seek. This is the “secret” that everyone is looking for when it comes to fitness.

Let’s assume you were to only read this particular entry of our Mastery Series and had no idea about the previous topics of Posture, Pace, or Path. And let’s assume you really dug in and took this strength training thing seriously and made it your goal to fully understand and implement this month’s topic of PURPOSE. If you were to have any level of success in doing so, you would automatically be on your way to mastering the others.

It is commonly known that the purpose of strength training is to create a stimulus and ultimately an adaptation, or basically to get stronger. But what we mean by ‘Purpose’ in the context of our protocol, has to do with our mental approach during the set. What is your true intent in the moment? Most of us are probably operating on an instinctive level. That’s to be expected. That’s how we’re “wired” so to speak. But here’s the problem with this approach. Our instincts do not want us to be struggling on a resistance training machine. Our instincts really don’t want us to struggle at all. This is known in the physiology world as our Perception of Effort and it acts to protect us, to limit our exertion from becoming harmful, and it’s a very valuable mechanism to have. But in order to get stronger and to truly progress over a lifetime, we need to operate with our intuition. At least during our exercise. We need to increase our tolerance to training or our Maximum Tolerable Perception of Effort. What’s the best way to go about doing this you might ask…by performing more strength training sessions!
We become more tolerant of training by training. This is the real secret that drives lifelong results.

Remember, the immediate goal of our exercise is to create a stimulative (i.e. significant) level of mechanical tension in as many muscle fibers of a muscle group as possible. In order to do this, we need to circumvent our protective instincts to some extent. We need to convince ourselves that what we are setting out to do is entirely volitional, expected, and even welcomed. When we talk ourselves out of continuing our effort we succumb to what is known in physiology as the Voluntary Activation Deficit. This means there’s a measurable difference between how much effort we could give versus the effort we actually give. The more effort we voluntarily give, the more muscle fibers we are going to access and activate, which is known as motor unit recruitment (MUR). This is important because a muscle fiber can only be stimulated if it is first activated. We control this activation (recruitment) through our voluntary effort.

This concept of motor unit recruitment brings us back to our Purpose. We need to be mentally engaged toward increasing our effort to the fullest extent possible. Any doubts or distractions will only derail our efforts, and ultimately our results. This helps explain why MSF has a climate controlled, distraction free environment, with constructive and actionable instruction from our trainers. It facilitates the focus required to maximize your effort. Pulling back the curtain a little, we can admittedly state that this level of focus is not required as a beginner. This is because as a beginner, anything you do above the level of effort you are accustomed to will invoke a stimulus. However, this is short lived and you will need to develop and progress your mental approach along the way, which our environment and supervision accommodates better than anyone.

Let us be your intuition…almost as though we are your copilot, guiding you toward continuous improvement in your exercise quality and intensity. The more attentive you are to the real objective and to our instruction the more likely you are to make this an automatic behavior. This can be a rewarding quest in other ways too as you will experience the benefit of being present, even if for only a handful of repetitions on an exercise. You’ll also be creating an ability to persevere through a challenging physical endeavor. This can create a more confident and capable mindset. While this isn’t necessarily our specialty, it's safe to say that these skills can transfer to other areas of the real world.

So in bringing all of this together, walk through the studio doors intent on having a laser-like focus on the instruction from your trainer and the quality of your execution. We will get you set with the correct Posture, lock it in place. We will help you establish the ideal Pace, maintain it at all costs. We will remind you to stay in a consistent movement Path, do not alter it. You should view every workout, every set, and every rep as an opportunity to practice staying attentive to these 3 components. And with these elements becoming more and more standardized, the fun part, the real challenge will be to add an unwavering intensity on top of this solid foundation. When you begin to pay attention to the details and implement the instruction from your trainer and push harder at the right moment because you know it will make a difference, you will begin to increase your maximum tolerable perception of effort, and most importantly, you will continue to truly experience all of the benefits that productive strength training has to offer.

topics.title: Gradual Load Up
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy 2/MSF Mastery Series - Issue 5 - Gradual Load Up.txt

blocks.text: With the Four P’s of Strength Training now established, let’s get a little more granular and begin to look at the nuts and bolts of our exercise execution. Before we do that however, let’s remind ourselves of the framework established by our Four P’s:
Posture - how we are positioned and braced during a movement.
Pace - the speed we are moving at any given moment in a set.
Path - the plane of motion our bodies travel through on an exercise.
Purpose - the real objective of resistance training. To subject as many muscle fibers to as much tension as we can create in that moment.

These are non-negotiable attributes of proper strength training and we must continue to cultivate our awareness of these if we’re ever going to make this a worthy, lifelong journey. Remember, your trainer is here to help you. It is what we are instructing you to do, moment to moment during your exercise here at MSF.

So let’s now add to that framework our first specific element of training in our Mastery Series, the gradual load up. Now this will likely have been one of the first things you were challenged with during your consultation, but chances are, you’ve forgotten about it. You would have been instructed to “gradually load up” or “slowly begin” on the Leg Press. But you were also instructed to do a dozen or so other things during the consult. And you are continually instructed to do dozens of other things during your workouts to the extent that the load up just seems to blend in to everything else.

But this is a chance to step back and consider this task in isolation, away from the anticipation of having to lift a heavy load and endure the struggle of the set. The load up is where a set of exercise truly begins. It's where the rubber meets the road so to speak. Left to our own devices (our instincts), our body will try and find the path of least resistance. This was discussed during the Four P’s series and here it is again. It seems our intuition is always at odds with our instincts. And if we’re not intentional, if we’re not receptive to instruction, our instincts will win every time. Without fail, we will hold our breath and heave into the load suddenly. This will almost always be followed by the explanation, “I just wanted to make sure I could lift it.”  Keep this in mind, if you cannot lift the load properly, it is the instructor’s fault, not yours.

Now, it's not as though a sudden load up is useless, or will not provide results, it will. But there are potential safety concerns if it becomes habitual. Remember at the end of the day, our body is responding to the amount or magnitude of mechanical tension experienced by the targeted muscles fibers. It does not respond to the magnitude of the load we are using or the number of reps we achieve. With this in mind, we want to focus on creating the highest amount of tension we can in the greatest number of targeted muscle fibers we can, all while keeping our joints safe. Well, this starts the moment we begin to apply pressure to the movement arm.

As the name implies, a gradual load up needs to happen gradually. This is different than slowly. Slowly refers to the speed at which we are moving. Gradual indicates a graded or incrementally increasing effort. So when instructed to gradually begin an exercise, think about what that means and how to go about doing exactly that. There needs to be a starting point where we begin to apply pressure with a slight enough effort that there is no movement yet. From there we need to build our force evenly until it reaches a point where it is just greater than the selected load. This is when the weight stack will begin to lift. Depending on the magnitude of the load, this can take anywhere from 2 to 6 seconds.

Think about that. We need to knowingly begin to push without any movement occurring and begin to build from there. Another way to think of it is as though you are trying to find the minimum level of force required to lift a weight. So if there were 100 pounds on the weight stack, we are trying to gradually find 101 pounds of pressure. That is a gradual load up. And that is not easy. It is also not an instinctively comfortable feeling. This can be overridden however with attentiveness and practice. So next time you are set to begin an exercise, listen for the instruction to “gradually begin to apply pressure” and think back to this installment of the Mastery Series. Challenge yourself to do exactly that…to gradually apply pressure. Notice the difference in the feeling that is produced. It won’t necessarily feel comfortable but it should feel productive. And you can be assured that you are on the right track to achieving all the benefits that strength training has to offer, before any movement has even occurred.

topics.title: Lower Turnarounds
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy 2/MSF Mastery Series - Issue 6 - Lower Turnarounds.txt

blocks.text: Continuing on with our Mastery Series, this month’s topic will focus on what we internally call the lower turnaround. You may have heard us refer to it during your sessions but if that term is unfamiliar, just know that it is the change of direction between the lowering of the weight and the lifting. So as you are lowering the weight, you then “turn around” and begin lifting.

Before we fully explore this particular attribute, let’s remind ourselves of why our Mastery Series is important, or should be at least, to our strength training. If we are to receive a benefit from these workouts, then we have to get better at them as they come up. When all of us first start our strength training journey, we have a sort of “beginner’s luck” that we can leverage where almost anything we do during our workouts will be stimulative (i.e. beneficial). This is because almost anything we do in the workout will most likely be at a level of exertion that we are NOT accustomed to. As a result, the body has to respond by increasing its level of strength and fitness.

But the more and more we exercise and the stronger we get, the less impactful the same level of effort will be in future workouts. We must continually challenge ourselves to train better, and this includes training harder. At the end of the day, we are trying to increase the number of muscle fibers we are activating (i.e. using) and the amount of tension they are subjected to. And this comes about through effort. But the effort cannot be random or haphazard or scattered. It needs to be directed. Specific muscular structures need to be loaded and kept under load for the duration of the set. And as the difficulty increases, we must do everything in our power to keep the targeted muscles loaded while increasing our effort.

Which brings us to the lower turnaround. This is likely the most challenging point in a single repetition on a given exercise. The lower turnaround is often where we have the least favorable leverage, which adds to difficulty in performing them correctly. This coupled with the fact that there seems to be additional discomfort in these positions as our muscles are in a somewhat lengthened or stretched state. However, if we are to succeed in our journey of continued strength and progress, we must conquer and master the lower turnaround.
There are three simple rules to properly performing a lower turnaround:
Always bottom out
Do not unload at the bottom
Do not fire out of the bottom

Importantly, when we say the “bottom” we are referring to the point in the movement that corresponds with the weight stack lowering and touching or bottoming out. Also note that there are some exercises where the weight stack may not touch, such as in a compound row or a pulldown. In these exercises, the bottom is defined by the elbows straightening. For most other movements, the weight stack should touch as you change directions.
THE THREE RULES OF THE LOWER TURNAROUND

Rule number one - always bottom out. If you’ve trained with us for any amount of time, you’ve surely heard us instruct to allow for a ”soft touch” or to “barely touch, barely start” at the bottom. And oftentimes we cannot see the weight stack as it is approaching this point. This is by design. This keeps us honest. It forces an even higher level of focus to have to sense the exact moment that this occurs. It also creates exponentially more tension because we are minimizing momentum, which requires the muscles to work harder. But keep in mind, this is a good thing. This is exactly what we are paying for from our workouts. As noted above and throughout the Mastery Series, tension is the stimulus we are seeking. Carefully lowering to just barely allow the weights to touch creates more tension than simply slamming them down or changing directions arbitrarily. So be attentive to our instruction and really challenge yourself to barely let the weights touch on movements that require it.

Rule number two - do not unload. It should go without saying that once we do allow the weights to touch softly, that we should not fully set them down or unload. This obviates the entire purpose of strength training, to create tension. But this also creates an instinctive battle that is hard to overcome. It's extremely difficult to slowly lower a weight, in a fatigued state, and remain attentive enough to only permit a soft touch without setting it down entirely and resting. As we’ve stated throughout the Mastery Series, consider every repetition of every workout as practice. You are practicing your strength training. There may not be a more worthwhile endeavor for humanity.

Rule number three - do not fire out. As equally challenging as lowering and only allowing the lightest touch of the weights is the requirement to not “fire out” of the bottom. This is all done with safety in mind first and foremost. Any sort of sudden forces can be injurious. We need to make sure we are pushing hard enough to change directions but not so hard that we introduce momentum. Again, this will require substantially more work from the muscles to manage properly. And there will be discomfort to overcome or at least minimize, but this discomfort is an inevitable byproduct of the tension. Most people will mistake the discomfort they feel with an inability to continue with their effort. This is where most will plateau. They will reach a certain, individual level of discomfort and will decide not to push anymore. Or even worse, they will decide to abruptly “fire out” of the bottom to get beyond the discomfort. Instead, push JUST HARD ENOUGH to change direction, without momentum.

All of this takes practice, so don’t expect each turn to be perfect, but execute with an intention of making each one perfect. The idea of “embracing the journey” has never been more applicable. Challenge yourself to focus entirely on the instruction you are receiving and your execution in the moment. Do not make this an emotional event for yourself. You are training with MSF to create a stronger, more resilient human existence. You must carry out the mission (workout) in a specific way to ensure the benefits. With this in mind, the more you work on perfecting your technique and specifically the lower turnarounds, the more readily you will accept and appreciate the struggle involved.

topics.title: Squeeze Technique
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy 2/MSF Mastery Series - Issue 7 - Squeeze Technique.txt

blocks.text: Hopefully by now, you’ve begun to implement some of the training insight that we’ve reintroduced through our MSF Mastery Series. The topics covered thus far are considered to be some of the foundational tenants of proper resistance training. If someone were to strength train for a portion of their lives with any amount of dedication, we might expect these to become automatic. But in order for that to happen they must first be known about and practiced with intent. Without these firmly engrained as habits, our progress is likely to be significantly limited. That’s why we urge you to come to each and every session with a qualitative mindset and a focus on the details. Which brings us to our next, and quite possibly most detailed topic yet in the Series, the “Squeeze” Technique.

If you have been listening to your trainer, you’ve undoubtedly heard them instruct you to “squeeze” on an exercise. But have you actually been squeezing? And in the manner that we would expect? And with the level of attention required to continue to ensure safety and progress? And what about after the squeeze…how do we resume the movement? Let’s attempt to answer all of these questions and more as we shed a little light on this often overlooked element of a set of exercise.

First and foremost, let’s establish what a squeeze actually is and why we would perform one. When we instruct you to squeeze, we are looking for you to continue the contraction of the targeted muscle (not the hands). Another way to think of it is to attempt to continue the movement without producing any external positional change. In other words, once you’ve reached the full range of motion on a repetition, you can continue to apply more force so that the muscle will contract harder without further movement. Take for instance, the leg extension. Once the knees are extended as straight as they will go, you cannot straighten them any further. However, what can be done is to ATTEMPT to continue to straighten them further. This will result in a stronger contraction of the thigh muscles. Importantly, this harder contraction in and of itself may not make for a more meaningful stimulus. So why bother?

The benefits that come from implementing and mastering the squeeze technique are both immediate and long-term. The squeeze creates another level of control required to display competency and ability to use the weight selected. If you cannot properly squeeze the targeted muscle(s) on an exercise that requires it, then you may not be ready to use that amount of weight. The squeeze becomes a proving ground where it is impossible to use a weight that would be considered excessive. If you cannot exaggerate your control with a given weight on a given exercise, you have more work to do to progress. And that’s a good thing. Remember, this is a lifelong endeavor of mastery.

In addition to the control and the resulting safety that a proper squeeze requires, there is a benefit to simply being aware of the targeted muscle(s). This will help not only on the current repetition but even more so by increasing motor unit recruitment in the long term. We’ve discussed motor unit recruitment in previous months’ lessons, and the importance of improving this through effort as we progress. This is important, you’ll remember, because unless a muscle fiber is active and contributing to a movement, it will not receive a benefit. By feeling a muscle and having an awareness of what we are targeting, we can increase the active number of muscle fibers. You receive more bang for your exercise buck so to speak.

Once you are in the squeeze position, and hopefully increasing your effort/force in an attempt to contract the muscle harder (i.e. squeezing), you then need to consider how to come out of that position. If you’ve been with MSF for any period of time you’ve likely been instructed to “ease out” following the click. Well, there is a lot more involved in this command than there may appear. Since we are in a static/stationary position of increasing effort, when our trainer ‘clicks’, we cannot yet resume movement. Our momentary effort is well above that which would permit us to begin lowering the weight. We must first carefully reduce our effort, while in the squeeze, to a level that is low enough that we can slowly begin to lower the weight with control. There is a necessary delay to gradually come out of the contracted position. If we are able to move immediately upon hearing the click, then we were probably not squeezing to begin with.

Which brings us to the point of this latest installment of the Mastery Series, the details matter. Or at least they should matter. The instruction your trainer provides is meant to guide you to become better at training. As mentioned before, this could very well be the most important skill you learn. So pay attention to the details and challenge yourself to be more precise with your training. Be gradual on your load ups. Be continuous on your turns. And be determined on your squeezes. Determined to ease into the contracted position, contract as hard as you can, and gradually “unsqueeze” as you slowly resume your movement.

One last point about the squeeze technique, it is important to note that it only occurs on certain exercises. And it is helpful to know what muscles you are targeting so that you can better focus on contracting them. This has always been and will always be a point of emphasis at MSF. Your trainer will guide you, just be present enough to receive the instruction and willing enough to implement it to the best of your ability.

OK, so you’ve been following along with the MSF Mastery Series, and you’ve been implementing the previous topics to the best of your abilities, and you’ve noticed your workouts are beginning to feel different. You feel more in control and intentional and you appreciate the challenge. Well, if you’ve made it this far and are wondering what's next, we thank you for taking this journey as seriously as you should. That alone will ensure your progress will be more than can be expected by simply “going through the motions”. But please understand that merely “going through the motions” will also lead to a multitude of health benefits. That’s what is so great about resistance training…the body doesn’t really have a choice when properly challenged. It has to adapt when presented with a stimulus. But for those looking for the next level of strength, resiliency, and longevity, you will need to become relentless in your training. And that’s what we are here for. We’re not only setting you up, keeping you safe, and tracking your sessions, but more importantly we are teaching you how to progressively train better, which is ultimately the most critical element of a strength training program. The qualitative improvement of the execution of the exercises themselves.

The term “better” can be interpreted in many ways, so allow us to clarify. Most people would assume that there is a quantitative measurement for a better workout. Either more weight or more reps or our favorite…more machines. But none of those are capable of measuring what really counts. None of those measure the actual stimulus that causes an adaptive change in the body. If it were that simple, our workouts could last all day and we would get more benefit than our bodies knew what to do with. But that really only requires more time and time is not stimulative in terms of strength or muscularity. It may work for fatigue resistance, otherwise known as endurance, but strength and muscle require a more precise stimulus. They require a certain level of intensity or effort to cause an adaptation. And for most of us, that is the hard part.

Our bodies are instinctively programmed to follow the path of least resistance. As a result, we tend to find the easy way out in many physical endeavors. This serves us well in potentially dangerous situations, acting as a protective, life-preserving mechanism. Unfortunately, this also limits our efforts during a workout. Our bodies do not know the difference between a challenging set of exercise or a life threatening situation. But the good news is that this ability can be cultivated and enhanced through practice. Our bodies/brains will get more tolerant and accepting of this higher level of effort. With more attentive and intentional sets of exercise comes more stimulative and beneficial workouts. With more attentive and intentional sets of exercise comes more strength, more resiliency, and longevity.

So how do we get there? We come to our sessions with the seriousness required of a life and death situation. While this may seem like a dramatic overstatement, when you genuinely work at this, you will begin to understand the comparison. Now, this is not meant to scare anyone away, because remember, this ability can be developed. See this as the “wake up call” that we alluded to in the Mastery Series Introductory article. But it takes practice. For starters, consider the following: instead of ruminating on the discomfort, focus on keeping your posture, your pace, and your path. Plant a seed in your subconscious that the struggle you are enduring is directly attributable to the benefits you seek. They are one in the same. Try and “allow” the discomfort for just one moment longer in each successive set of exercise. By keeping your attention fixated on your posture, pace, and path, you will engrain a more productive mindset. You will no longer talk yourself out of the hard part. The important part. You may even begin to thrive in these situations. We plan on training this way for the rest of our lives and we hope you will be right there with us along the way.

By focusing our attention on external factors, we can expect to become more robotic and less emotional. We can actually practice being more present, which apparently is something we could all use more of anyway. Let the workout become that for you. Now the most important external factor when it comes to training harder is without a doubt, maintaining your PACE! Yes, we move “slowly” here at MSF. You’ll notice slowly is in quotes. That’s because speed is relative. Our pace isn’t necessarily slow, especially when you are training with a high level of effort. You’ll soon find that while we appear to be moving slowly to the average onlooker, internally we are pushing pretty darn hard. Hard enough that you would expect the weight (or movement arm of the machine) to be moving faster. And this is where the magic happens. Ideally we will reach a point in our set of exercise where the machine will begin to “bog down” or slow down on us, despite our greatest effort to maintain our pace. This is precisely the point in the set where our muscle fibers are experiencing a level of tension that is stimulative. This basically means our muscles are working hard enough to invoke the physiological stimulus we seek. We need to make a voluntary decision to push harder when the movement arm we are pushing against begins to involuntarily slow down on us. Read that last sentence again. Think about what it's really saying. If it isn’t clear now, don’t worry, just keep coming to your sessions prepared to learn and improve (Kaizen!). We will help to simplify the science.

All of these Mastery Series articles are essentially leading to the point made above. They are all a piece of the same puzzle. And if we as a species are to reap the benefits of what has been rightly termed “The Fountain of Youth” we need to look beyond the simple recommendations provided in the articles and posts that commonly come our way. In order for this stuff to actually work, it has to be done in a truly productive manner. And more importantly over time, it has to trend with an increasingly higher level of intensity. Now, because of this, it doesn’t get easier but you will find that you become more accepting of the struggle. You have made the connection to the benefits you have and will continue to receive for your efforts. You will feel more sense of purpose and accomplishment from these endeavors and you will begin to fully embody this most challenging way of training. You may even begin to notice the physical prowess and mental clarity that come through regular bouts of exertion. As we’ve stated throughout this Series, we are here to guide you. That’s essentially what you are paying us for and we are excited to show you the way! Be forewarned however, this will become addicting. You can thank us later…welcome to the club.

Well you wouldn’t think we would have to write about this latest topic. After all, breathing is an involuntary activity that happens whether we want it to or not thanks to our autonomic nervous system. But for some reason, we refuse to let nature take its course when we are exerting. And even when prompted by our instructor to “breathe”, we decide to override this wise advice and do the opposite. We bear down and hold our breath. Now it's not entirely your fault…we are programmed to do exactly this as a protective mechanism.

You see, in the moment, holding our breath allows for a temporary increase in force production. So why wouldn’t we take advantage of this? Well there are a couple of reasons. For one, and most importantly, this ValSalva maneuver as it is technically called can be potentially dangerous for those with certain pre-existing medical conditions, particularly those involving the heart, brain, or eyes. It should be avoided at all costs.

Secondly, while a well timed ValSalva maneuver may get us through a more challenging part of a set of exercise (think bottom of the leg press), because we are sustaining a continuous effort we need to continuously breathe to support this effort. This will keep us “in the running” as we like to say for a longer period of time as we are more likely to be able to keep up with the cardiovascular demands of the set. Now for those of you that have been indoctrinated into proper training over the years might point out, while we are not necessarily looking for a longer set, we do want to be able to last long enough to create a stimulus. And although it is not time dependent, if we quit or run out of breath before we are truly pushing hard enough (i.e. involuntary slowing) to create high levels of mechanical tension, it may not be a productive set.

One last reason to breathe continuously would be to avoid using more than just the required muscles to perform the given movement pattern. By holding our breath, we tend to tense up other muscles to create more stability throughout the body. While this does make us potentially stronger in that moment, we are also using our limited nervous system capacity to contract otherwise uninvolved muscles. This limits the motor unit recruitment signal that could be sent to the intended target muscles resulting in a weaker and most likely insufficient stimulus. So keep breathing and try not to turn every exercise into a full body, global effort. This takes practice but with time you can unlock new levels of progress.

The next question might be, “how exactly should we breathe” or maybe “I feel like I am breathing, what am I doing wrong”? The brief moments of breath holding almost always go unnoticed by the trainee. They are often disguised by a rapid catch up period of over breathing. Additionally, because they are more likely to happen during when greater effort is required and the trainee is under duress, they will be completely unaware of whether or not they are breathing. For the record, any restriction of breathing goes against what we are suggesting. Those of you that like to blow air are restricting your breathing. Those that like to breathe through clenched teeth or pursed lips are also restricting your breathing. And the most overtly improper technique of grunting, groaning, verbalizing, etc. is nothing more than holding your breath to gain a mechanical advantage. It is not a sign of power or effort, but rather wasted energy that attempts to make the exercise easier.

Our challenge to you would be similar to all of the other Mastery Series topics. Come to every workout with an intent on being more focused and attentive to our instruction. When we suggest to you to “breathe more” as you are in the eccentric (lowering) phase headed toward and through the lower turn, make a conscious effort to do exactly that. It won’t be easy and your muscles will have to work harder. But that’s why we train. And if we are going to train regularly, we might as well try and train better.

Another simple piece of advice might be to just avoid holding your breath. While it may take more mental effort to think about how to breathe, maybe it makes more sense for you to just ensure you are not holding your breath. Besides, most of us go through the other 23.5 hours of the day never once thinking about our breathing. We just let it happen. Well, that might be the best approach when training at MSF. And just like the rest of our day, when we increase our effort, like walking faster, or going up stairs, our breathing will increase on its own. We don’t need to think about it for it to happen. Well the same applies with our training. As your effort increases, so should your breathing. Remember, we want to keep you safe first and foremost here at MSF but we also want you to continue to improve with your technique and your results. As always, talk with your trainer about these topics and let's truly take control of our strength and longevity!

blocks.text: So if you’ve made it this far in the MSF Mastery Series, to our 10th and final edition, we thank you. You will make our job easier and more rewarding. Chances are you have become more knowledgeable on and interested in the topic of strength training. You’ve likely become more receptive to our instruction and as a result, you see it as more meaningful and your workouts are now more productive. And while we’re calling it our final edition, it’s really just the final for now. There will certainly be other topics to discuss and even revisions of older ones as we gain new insights and perspectives on strength training. If this is the first one you are reading, welcome, but we would suggest you start with the first one and read through sequentially. While each topic does address a stand alone quality, it would make sense from an implementation perspective to start at the beginning. Our intent was to introduce one topic at a time and then work to put that topic to use for the month so it becomes more automatic. The next topic would then be added to the previous, which is already ingrained (or at least well on its way).

Because what we do here at MSF is so drastically different, we thought it would be a good idea to give a little more insight into the science behind how resistance training works and how the body responds to the stimulus. Most of the commonly held beliefs about working out directly oppose our methodology and it’s almost hard to believe that the general consensus could be so wrong. You’ve probably shared the idea of our approach with family and friends and were almost certainly met with confusion or disbelief. We know, we struggle with that every day in our introduction to prospective clients. So that’s what inspired this latest volume of the Mastery Series. Let this arm you with a little more knowledge and at the same time provide you with even more reassurance that what you are doing is the best thing you can do from a physical measure outside of medical intervention!

It makes sense though, that most people would think that what they believe about strength training is factual. We’ve relied on faulty beliefs and “bro science” for decades. And while there is a ton of detail to consider for an understanding of human physiology, we believe it can all be supported by a simple framework. At least in terms of our protocol and how to implement it in the most optimal way. And in this case that simple framework consists of the physiological mechanisms that create responses, or stimuli, in the body. These are some of the things that will be discussed throughout this issue.
The Common Beliefs

So in establishing a framework, a good place to start is to dispel some of the more commonly held beliefs about strength training. For one, those with a surface level orientation to strength training will tell you that muscle is built by first being torn down and then rebuilt stronger. This is often the only requirement proclaimed for building muscle. In stating this most popular attribute, they are missing the two other mechanisms that are commonly stated as fact by the more well studied coaches, trainers, or physiologists. Those two other avenues to muscle building would be, metabolic stress and mechanical tension. So here we have it, the three ways to build muscle that has been passed around for decades:
Muscle damage
Metabolic stress
Mechanical tension

And the result of having these three mechanisms available for muscle building is that most of the workouts and strategies have been designed to encapsulate all three. Why not, right? It would seem to make sense that the more poles we have in the water so to speak, the better the chance we have at achieving results. The more muscle we should build and the faster we should build that muscle.

Because the variety mechanisms discussed above were accepted as not only true but required for building muscle, typical workout strategies would include excessive volume in an effort to capture all of the potential benefits. They would have multiple sets of the same exercises and multiple exercises per muscle group to create the coveted soreness or damage. They would also include high reps for the metabolic stress “finisher” or “burn” that we’re all so familiar with. And for the last one, mechanical tension, many would want to also include some heavier sets. So when you add all that up, you have quite a lot of volume. Way too much really, and it’s not only unnecessary but detrimental as the fatigue created from that amount of work will most certainly diminish the benefits.
What We Know to be True

Now that we know the common beliefs and how those may have shaped the traditionally prescribed workout protocols, let’s take a look at what we now know to be true and how that changes things. First and foremost, there is only one driver of hypertrophy…Mechanical Tension. The other mechanisms were disproved by testing each one in the absence of mechanical tension and observing the results. In either case, damaging a muscle or injecting it with metabolites, there was no addition or growth of muscle tissue. In the case of muscle damage, the hormonal response is similar to that from a workout but the net effect is simply to clear the resulting inflammation from the damage and repair the muscle fiber to its original state. And when a muscle is injected with lactic acid for example, there is no muscular growth. These are both side effects of training but not stimuli for growth. Only with mechanical tension is muscular growth stimulated.

So at this point, you might be wondering, what exactly is mechanical tension and how does it lead to building muscle (i.e. hypertrophy)? Mechanical tension is a physical pulling force experienced by individual muscle fibers. Muscle fibers overlap when they contract and this is accomplished by the actin and myosin filaments sliding over top of each other, or overlapping. In other words, muscles “pull” on bones to move them when they contract and this pulling force is what creates mechanical tension. Technically, mechanical tension will be present in any muscular contraction performed by the body. But if we are lifting a cup of coffee and therefore producing mechanical tension, is that really going to make us stronger or build muscle?

The answer to that question is obviously ‘no’. So then how does mechanical tension actually lead to hypertrophy? The key to this most important question lies in something known as the force-velocity relationship of skeletal muscle. Simply stated, as the velocity of movement decreases, the force that can be produced increases. There is an inverse relationship. So lifting a relatively heavy weight slowly (low velocity) requires a more maximal force. Importantly however, this low velocity movement has to be involuntarily slow. Here are a couple of ways to conceptualize this:

The speed of movement of the machine one is lifting begins to slow down despite the effort to maintain the pace or accelerate. Think about the footplate on a leg press and how it “bogs down” on us as we’re fatiguing. If we cannot lift it any faster, we will have a higher level of mechanical tension present.

It is more simply stated as training to or near muscular failure, which for our purposes happens at concentric failure. In other words, the reps closest to the end of a set tend to slow down until we can no longer lift the weight. And while many believe that failure occurs when the involved muscles are fully “fatigued” or “torn down”, that is not the case. This is another fallacy that was never linked to a mechanism. Instead, we reach our maximum tolerable perception of effort via a protective signal sent to the brain. This can be a topic for a future volume in the Mastery Series for anyone that may want to know more!

The slower movement results from a slower contraction velocity in the muscle. Because of this slow velocity, the muscle fiber components stay attached longer rather than pulling and releasing almost instantly as occurs in faster movements. By hanging on longer, there are more connections made, which creates a greater pulling force from the muscle. And this higher level of pulling force is what creates the potential for stimulative levels of mechanical tension in the active muscle fibers. That last part is critical and it is a foundational concept to understanding the physiology of strength training. And that is that a muscle fiber cannot be stimulated until it is first activated by a signal sent from the central motor command of the brain. This is known as motor unit recruitment (MUR) and the magnitude of our MUR is governed by our effort. The greater the effort the greater the MUR. And one of the more interesting ideas in resistance training is that our highest possible levels of MUR can be increased with progressively higher levels of effort over time. So we can increase our upper limit. Read those last two sentences again! In fact this must happen if we are to keep making progress. The take home here is that in an indirect way, the whole purpose of training is to become better at training; to become more tolerant of training; and to get a better effect from training.

In considering all of the above, we can now have a better understanding of why excessive volume, soreness, muscle damage, high reps, etc. are not only unnecessary but detrimental to the results we seek. As mentioned above, the fatigue caused from all of those typical workout attributes compete for resources with the muscle building stimulus. There will be a lot more to discuss on this topic too if you are interested. The critical component to understanding this is that once we create the stimulus, more reps/sets/tension will not necessarily lead to a larger stimulus. Once a muscle is stimulated, it would be best to move onto training another muscle group.

C. Finishing a set with a static - For those subjects that do not reach apparent concentric failure, we will often end the set with an attempt to achieve a higher level of intensity. This is usually in the form of a static hold in a leveraged but still challenging position where the instructor will encourage them to keep working while counting them down. On the following four compound pushing movements (also continuous as indicated above) it is best to have the subject perform their last complete or nearly complete repetition, and then at the approximate midpoint of the final eccentric have them pause.
Leg Press
Chest Press
Overhead Press
Seated Dip

A count of 5 to 10 seconds is usually performed here while the subject works to hold their midpoint position. Again, this is in lieu of the preferred course of training to concentric failure. Importantly, all other movements outside of the four listed above, are usually best intensified by having the subject hold the last rep in the contracted position while the instructor counts them down. The only exceptions would be the Cervical and Lumbar Extensions. A normal 2 to 3 second count in the contracted position makes more sense for these two movements because we are not seeking a high level of intensity with them.

Abdominals

Torso Rotation

When deciding whether to add an exercise to a client’s program, the Exercise Practitioner must evaluate several factors. The goal is not simply to increase the number of exercises performed, but to ensure that every addition improves the client’s results and experience without compromising the quality or intensity of the workout.
The following framework should guide the decision making process.
Key Questions Before Adding an Exercise
Will the addition improve or maintain the appropriate training frequency for the targeted muscles?
Will the exercise provide sufficient overlap in the muscle fibers being trained if different exercises are used between workouts?
Does the addition address a goal or concern expressed by the client, either verbally or through their intake information (demographics)?
Is there sufficient time/room available in the workout to perform the exercise with proper control and execution?
Can the client maintain the necessary intensity of effort if another exercise is added?
Will the addition improve the overall client experience without compromising training quality?

Each of these factors should be considered carefully before expanding a program. Keep in mind that most clients typically perform at least 6 exercises per workout (after the initial “learning curve” period of around 4 to 6 workouts). More advanced subjects might be able to perform 8 exercises or possibly more in a session. The points outlined below will help determine how to calibrate session volume on a client by client basis.
1. Training Frequency
A twice per week stimulus is necessary to optimize long term muscular adaptations.

Strength itself is not an adaptation but rather the outcome of a multitude of underlying adaptations, many of which are neurological. Because of this, strength can often be built or maintained with a once per week stimulus to that specific movement pattern.

Muscle growth, however, requires more consistent stimulation. Some hypertrophy will occur initially with a once per week workout, but progress will typically plateau soon after the base level adaptations are achieved.

Training once per week is still beneficial. Strength can be maintained and sometimes improved, and some muscle can be built or maintained. However, if the goal is to optimize muscular development and long-term progress, a twice per week stimulus is the more effective approach.

When deciding whether to add an exercise, the practitioner should consider whether the addition will help ensure that the targeted muscle groups (and more specifically, muscle fibers) are being stimulated twice per week.
2. Fiber Specific Adaptation and Exercise Overlap
Hypertrophy occurs within individual muscle fibers that experience sufficient mechanical tension.
If a muscle fiber is not recruited and exposed to meaningful mechanical tension, it will not benefit from the workout.

This principle has important implications for program design. Only the muscle fibers that are recruited in both workouts of the week will receive the necessary frequency of stimulation for optimal progress.
If certain hip muscles, for example, are stimulated in only one workout but not the second, the progress of those muscles will not reach full potential.
For this reason, performing the exact same exercises in both workouts is often the most reliable way to ensure that the same fibers are being trained consistently.

However, clients often prefer some variation in their programming. When variation is introduced, the practitioner must ensure that there is still substantial overlap in the muscle groups we wish to emphasize.

An example would be performing a pulldown in one workout and performing a pullover combined with a biceps curl in the other workout. In this case, the latissimus dorsi and biceps are still being trained in both sessions.

The key point is that if exercises differ between workouts, there must still be meaningful overlap in the muscle fibers being trained. And this becomes increasingly important as a subject becomes more advanced.
3. Client Feedback and Requests
Most clients will eventually express curiosity or interest in additional exercises or machines.

These requests may appear in several ways. A client may ask when they will be able to try other machines in the studio. They may express concern that a particular area of their body is not receiving enough attention. They may state, for instance, that they “feel their midsection needs more work”, or they may simply say that they would like to “do more machines”.

In these situations the Exercise Practitioner must be listening and ensure that the client feels heard. They should also be prepared to teach and inform and teach the client the fundamentals of resistance training including exercise selection and programming. The points made throughout this document and the entire MSF Academy are the considerations to be made for client education.

From the beginning of the client relationship, the practitioner should emphasize the importance of quality execution and effort rather than the number or variety of exercises performed. Clients should understand that results are driven by effort and mechanical tension applied to the muscles, not by the number of machines used during a workout. Importantly, the emphasis of quality over quantity is the primary attribute of the MSF protocol that helps to ensure the safety of each and every client.

At the same time, delivering a remarkable client experience is a priority. If a requested exercise can be added without compromising the quality or effectiveness of the workout, it is often appropriate to accommodate the request. Just expect that it will most likely have to become part of the routine moving forward in order to be effective and not just an occasional inclusion when requested.
The practitioner must balance education with responsiveness to the client’s interests.
4. Client Goals from the Demographics Packet
Exercise Practitioners should be very familiar with the information contained in the client’s demographics or intake form.

Clients frequently list goals such as strengthening the core, toning the arms, or improving overall strength. If a client takes the time to complete this form, it is important that the program clearly addresses the concerns they identified.
These goals should be discussed early in the client’s journey. The practitioner should explain which exercises in the program are intended to address those goals.

As discussed previously, targeted muscle groups should ideally be trained twice per week. In many cases this will mean performing the same exercise in both workouts in order to ensure consistent stimulation of the relevant muscle fibers.
Ensuring that client goals are clearly addressed in the exercise selection process can significantly improve client relationships and engagement.
5. Time Constraints Within the Workout
Every workout has a practical time limit.
When new clients begin training, the loads used are typically lighter in order to allow them to learn proper technique and develop control of the equipment.

Lighter loads generally lead to longer sets, often exceeding ten repetitions. Because of this, sets tend to take longer to complete and the total number of exercises that can be performed within the workout is limited.
During this stage of training the primary focus should be on precise execution and exaggerated control of the load.

It is important to remember that twenty minutes is the minimum amount of time for a workout, not the standard amount of time. Instructors should not rush or eliminate exercises in an effort to complete the workout sooner (i.e. within 20 minutes).

As clients accumulate training experience they often become capable of producing the desired stimulus with heavier loads and fewer repetitions. As set durations shorten, additional exercises may become feasible within the available time.

This progression should be explained to clients early in their training experience. Practitioners should reinforce that quality execution is always the priority and that there may be opportunities to expand the program as the client becomes more advanced.

If a requested exercise can easily be added without compromising quality or time constraints, it may be appropriate to include it. However, the practitioner should not allow the program to be dictated entirely by the client’s desire to use more machines.
6. Intensity Limits Within the Workout
Just as every workout has a time limit, every workout should also have an intensity limit.

Advanced clients who train with precision and focus are capable of generating very high levels of effort. Because of this, there is a practical limit to the number of exercises that can be performed at the intensity required to create a meaningful stimulus.
Performing an additional exercise does not automatically lead to additional benefit. A certain level of intensity is required for an exercise to be productive.
There is an inverse relationship between intensity and volume. As the intensity of effort increases, the total amount of work that can be performed decreases.

For a highly focused and experienced client performing seven or eight exercises with appropriate intensity, it becomes increasingly unlikely that additional exercises can be added without reducing the quality of effort.

While there may be occasional exceptions, the instructor should carefully observe the client’s effort level and remind them that their focus should be on getting more out of the exercises they are already performing rather than simply adding more exercises/volume.
As training experience increases, the importance of intensity of effort becomes even greater to insure a stimulus.
7. Establishing Authority and Building Trust
Exercise Practitioners should position themselves as knowledgeable authorities in strength training, but this authority must be earned through trust.
Trust is built through listening carefully to clients and approaching each interaction with genuine interest and empathy.
Practitioners should listen first and then look to inform/educate.

If a client raises a question that the practitioner cannot immediately answer, it is appropriate to acknowledge the question and indicate that further research or discussion with colleagues will be conducted. The instructor should then follow up with the client as soon as possible with a well informed response.

Additionally, the usefulness and insightfulness of the practitioner’s instruction goes a long way in establishing credibility with the clients. The MSF team should constantly strive to master their craft through reading, meetings, and discussion on various training topics. It is imperative in this profession that an instructor continue to stay engaged and add to their skill base.
This process strengthens trust and reinforces the professionalism of the MSF team.

When trust has been established, clients are more likely to accept guidance regarding the structure of their workouts, including decisions about whether additional exercises should or should not be included.

In some cases, a client may feel that a muscle group is not being addressed or that the workouts are “not challenging”. More often than not, the true issue is that the exercise is not being performed with enough intensity and/or proper technique. In these situations the solution will be improved execution rather than additional exercises and the practitioner must first be aware and then convincing enough to communicate this. Trust will only help the instructor in these situations.
Quality execution should always remain the priority.
Final Perspective

Every decision regarding exercise selection should support two goals. The first is delivering the most efficient, effective, and safe training stimulus possible. The second is providing a remarkable experience for every client during every workout.
Adding an exercise to a program is often the easiest decision to make. However, this should only occur after careful consideration of the factors outlined in this document.
Exercise Practitioners are not simply guiding clients through workouts. They are teaching a skill that can significantly influence long term health and physical capability.
Because of this, the practitioner must demonstrate attention to detail, thoughtful program design, and a clear commitment to the client’s success.

When this approach is consistently applied, clients begin to recognize that the practitioner cares more about the workout than they do. Over time this perspective helps shift the client’s focus away from quantity and toward the quality of effort and execution that ultimately drives progress.

The following document can be used as a guideline when determining which exercises to incorporate for the Initial Consultation as well as when establishing an initial A and B routine for a variety of client types. In some situations, a client may come to us down the road with a new goal or concern, in which case we can begin to modify their routine accordingly.

The most sensible place to start will be the client’s intake form (demographics) where they will list any orthopedic issues or concerns they have along with any goals or target areas they would like to address. This form, in addition to the discussions we have with them during the consultation or in subsequent sessions will provide insight as to what movement patterns will be most beneficial. Keep in mind that from a very high level, a conservative would be to simply select one movement from each of the following five categories:

However, in an effort to be more responsive to the client’s needs and goals, please consider the following commonly reported/requested conditions and the possible exercises to include when constructing a relevant training program. Keep in mind these are just suggestions and can be used more for guidelines or ideas rather than formal rules. Importantly, the last column, “Eventual A + B”, would be something that should be progressed to over the course of several months or more. Again, it is included here simply to show how a routine MIGHT evolve over time. Additionally, in any of the situations below, an eighth or possibly ninth exercise can be added to any of the workouts (key exercises should be repeated in the A and B) to make for a more complete/customized routine.
Programming and/or sequencing to potentially avoid:

LE+LP - Leg Extension and Leg Press in the same session tends to be a lot of quadriceps stimulus. This should rarely be used for our clients especially those that are intensity adverse or in the older demographic. These two exercises would be more beneficial on two non-consecutive days as we are ensuring a more frequent stimulus for the quads while allowing enough time for recovery. If we do decide to include in the same workout, make sure it is what the client needs and do not push to failure on both exercises (or either) when introducing. This should be discussed with the Studio Leader before implementing.

Lumb→LP - Performing Lumbar directly into Leg Press should be avoided as the fatigue from the lumbar exercise will invariably carry over into the leg press. Even when the lumbar is performed at a lower intensity. This can be an extremely uncomfortable feeling for the wrong reasons. The instructor may find the complementary pairing of Lumbar with Leg Extension (instead of LP) to be beneficial.

Lumb→LC - During a properly executed Leg Curl, there will be a tendency to extend the lower back, especially as effort increases. If we complete a set of Lumbar Extension immediately before the Leg Curl, the fatigue in the lower back will tend to make the extension required on the LC extremely uncomfortable. Especially for those subjects that are sensitive to spinal extension. For this reason, it may be better advised to program these two movements in separate workouts.

LP/LE→Lumb/Abs - Performing any quadriceps movement directly into Lumbar can be quite uncomfortable on the quadriceps because of the pressure from the femur restraint mechanism. Additionally, the Lumbar requires a higher level of technical proficiency and control as a means of ensuring safety. When the lower body has been fatigued immediately beforehand, it makes the Lumbar exercise harder to accurately perform.

Pd→CR or CR→Pd - When two pulling movements are back to back in a workout, the gripping muscles will likely be the limiting factor. For many subjects, the gripping muscles are already a limiting factor with just one pulling movement. If the gripping muscles are extremely weak, we can be assured that they will adapt to grow stronger over time just as any other muscle will that is progressively challenged.

Lumb+Abs/Torso Rotation - Lumbar with Abdominals in the same workout can be problematic from the standpoint of the immediate effect of weakening of the core/trunk musculature. If one were to perform Lumbar first, the fatigue experienced in the low back would be present while performing the abdominal exercise. Since abdominals are ultimately trunk flexion, the low back is required to round/stretch, which can be uncomfortable after having been trained. Furthermore, the subject is likely to sense that the lower back is fatigued, which then becomes their point of focus. A similar consequence will be had if the Abdominals are trained prior to the Lumbar muscles in the same workout. Having said all of this, it may still be beneficial in some situations to include both movements in the same workout. If a client is only training with us once per week and we wish to address both sets of muscles, it would be permissible to include both exercises. Additionally, there is a therapeutic effect that we can create training both movement patterns in the same workout. If this is the case, it seems through experience that performing the Abdominal exercise first with the Lumbar performed several exercises later is the best approach. Basically, having fatigued abdominals going into Lumbar exercise is a more conservative approach then having fatigued lumbar muscles going into the Abdominal exercise. Additionally, both weights should be conservatively set and because this will be used as a more therapeutic approach, we are not looking for a high intensity effort. Use this approach with caution and involve your Studio Leader and/or MSF Corp to devise a strategy.

Any push→push or pull→pull - This is commonly known as a prefatigue in the strength training world. And while it has been popularized specifically by the high intensity faction, it is based on the faulty premise that fatigue is a stimulus for hypertrophy. Recall that mechanical tension is the only documented driver of hypertrophy and that importantly, only a recruited motor unit can experience tension. If we are training overlapping muscle groups (i.e. muscle fibers) back to back, there will undoubtedly be some fatigue present from the exercise before. This fatigue acts to reduce the motor unit recruitment (MUR) in the targeted muscle group(s) and as a result, the potential stimulus is diminished. Because of this, it is optimal to train non-overlapping muscles in consecutive sets. For instance, we would not want to perform a chest flye into the chest press, as the output possible in the chest press will be greatly reduced. Same with compound row into pulldown or leg extension into leg press. All of these pairings present the same problem; a reduction in MUR, which has negative consequences in terms of creating a stimulus.
Discussion on number of exercises

In the above examples you’ll notice that most of the workouts were constructed with 7 exercises. This should eventually be the average number of exercises in a session. Keep in mind that as MSF Exercise Practitioners, we want to provide a REMARKABLE experience for every client and every workout. Part of that experience can be attributed to the fact that the workout should last at least 20 minutes and even longer than that in a majority of cases.

For a relatively new client, 5 exercises should likely take longer than 20 minutes for a couple of reasons. Firstly, we should be intentionally underestimating the strength of the new client in an effort to allow them to learn how to control their movement without being completely overwhelmed. It should still be challenging as the set progresses, which would most likely land them at a 10 - 12 or more rep set. In addition to the higher number of reps contributing to a longer session, a new client will require the setup of each exercise along with more instruction and explanation. There will typically be discussions after each set too to reinforce the important concepts for our training protocol. Remember, we are teaching them an invaluable skill.

As a client progresses in their understanding and their level of strength, the instructor can challenge them with more load. As the load increases, the reps will decrease into the 6 to 10 range, which would be considered ideal for MOST (not all) clients. Along with that, they will require virtually no setup time and there will be limited instruction necessary as they will have been learning this whole time. As a result, the time per exercise will decrease, which will be more conducive to performing 6 to 8 exercises during the half hour time period.
