The short answer…? You will end up at the same place if you are training to or at least near failure, so from a high level perspective, it does not matter. But here's what does matter:
Higher Reps (approx 10 plus) create a higher level of perceived effort through:
More reps = more fatigue
Increased cardiovascular demand
Increased afferent feedback (discomfort, lactic acid, "burn")
Longer duration, more mentally taxing

Perceived effort limits the level of motor unit recruitment that can be achieved in any maximal effort contraction. Simply stated, the more we "feel" any discomfort, the fewer muscle fibers we will be able to activate/recruit/use. This is known as the maximum level of tolerable effort...we just can't tolerate any more. And this likely happens well before we get the required stimulus we seek from training (mechanical tension).

So this would lead us to believe that heavier weight and fewer reps are superior. The problem with this approach is that most people are not capable of handling a "heavier" weight that brings them to failure in 5 to 7 reps. They don't have the ability to control that amount of load and they require more "practice" with lighter loads and higher reps.

Usually with newer clients, we will automatically default to lighter weights for purposes of learning all of the qualitative elements we require (posture, pace, path) and particularly the lower turnarounds. Over time, we begin to increase the loads and their reps should come down, but only to the extent that they maintain their form. Oftentimes we'll reach a point where the client begins to wrestle the weight rather than use it with control. We need to constantly remind them that there is a standard of quality to maintain. But if I have a client that is compliant and follows instruction, I will absolutely try and progress them to a lower rep range.
Am I getting stronger?

Aside from asking “was that more weight?” asking “am I getting stronger?” seems to be one of the more frequently asked questions. And while we could simply answer yes or no…they would most likely require further explanation to satisfy them. With this being the case, a little background information is necessary for perspective.

Firstly, anyone engaging in a properly designed, safely performed, progressively challenged strength training program can expect to get stronger. This is especially true for those that haven't done any sort of strength training in the recent past. So most assuredly we can answer “yes” to that inquiry. But the reason they are asking must be because they are unaware themselves or need to be convinced. This is an unfortunate occurrence.

It could be that the person asking lives a relatively inactive life, in which case they would not have an opportunity to notice or prove to themselves that they have in fact gotten stronger. Again, this is unfortunate but probably not that uncommon. But if this is the case, then any amount of strength training done with any level of intensity should represent a profound “wake up call” of sorts. Or it could be that this particular individual is just physically unaware of themselves, which would tend to be the case for a good number of our clients as that is what possibly drew them to MSF in the first place. In other words, they don’t know how to tell or measure their new levels of strength and want an objective measurement from the workout chart. While the answer would be, “yes, you are lifting more weight than you did when you started,” that can be a little misleading.

It can almost be guaranteed that one will go on to lift more weight at MSF than when they first joined. Part of the reason is because we will start conservatively with them, using significantly lighter weights than they are currently capable of lifting to facilitate the learning process. It takes time and attention to learn how to properly strength train and our focus is always on the qualitative approach. So the relative light weights that we start with will soon be surpassed as the client learns how to control their movement and effort. In this case, it is likely that they have gotten stronger as the neurological adaptations alone that take place very quickly, on a rep-to-rep basis at times, are a big component of getting stronger. On a side note, strength itself is not an adaptation, but rather an outcome. There are 6 or more adaptations that go into making someone stronger of which neurological efficiency and muscle mass are two of the major ones.

Now in the case of an advanced client that has been training for 3 - 5 years or more, there is a chance that they have reached their genetic “ceiling” in terms of strength. In fact everyone is likely to reach this point if they subject themselves to enough stimulus (i.e. training sessions). But once we reach this point, it would make zero sense to stop training as we would then begin to lose our strength. So it’s best to just keep training without concern for a genetic limit. Just assume that it doesn’t even exist, keep training, and at least maintain as much strength as you can for the rest of your life.

All of that to say that the real bottleneck in all of this usually comes down to the willingness or tolerance of the client to produce a truly hard and adaptive effort. When someone first begins a strength training program (or any physical activity for that matter), almost everything will be stimulative as it will be at a level above what they are currently used to. However, as one gets stronger, the current level of effort will not be enough to surpass the newfound level of strength. A harder, more intense effort is required to keep progressing. This is a simple biological adaptation model. The more someone has engaged in training, the higher the level of output is required to be stimulative. But the good news is, with more training comes more ability and tolerance and skill. The subject should be capable of training harder because of the practice of training and the instruction they receive. This is the primary purpose of an Exercise Practitioner. Aside from ensuring their safety of course.

There should be no doubt to the subject that they themselves have gotten stronger if they are consistently training with us and they are focused on their intensity and technique. They should be able to feel the difference proper strength training makes by just standing there with an awareness. If not and we need to point to other examples, we have gotten plenty of input over the years:
Posture
Less joint pain
Getting out of bed
Up and down stairs
Getting in and out of the car
Golfing
Carrying groceries
Lifting up children
Yardwork
Opening doors
Walking through stores or the neighborhood
Loading/unloading items from the trunk
Getting off the floor
Getting out of a chair
Lifting suitcase into overhead storage

All of these would be indicative of an increase in strength. They are all also improved with practice as any physical endeavor is specific. If one wants to get better at going up and down stairs or getting off the floor, these should be carefully practiced. The strength increase will make all of those things easier but the point being that there is also a skill component.

So to sum up, yes, everyone that begins training with us will assuredly become stronger. The question is, how much and to what degree? And this is entirely up to the individual. How seriously will they take their sessions and the instruction? How much will they challenge themselves to get better at strength training? The Instructor will not hold them back and they will even encourage, but ultimately it is up to the client to decide how hard they want to work over time. In this way, they will not ever have to question whether they are getting stronger, they will give their body no choice.
I don’t want to get “bulky” ( I just want to get more “toned”)
The muscular response to resistance training is genetically mediated and it cannot be changed.
Osteoporosis, Osteopenia, and Bone Density Concerns
Is strength training safe if I have osteoporosis or osteopenia?

Yes, when it is done correctly and under proper supervision. At MaxStrength Fitness, exercises are controlled, customized to your abilities, and progressed gradually. This allows your muscles and bones to adapt safely without unnecessary strain.
Can strength training actually improve bone density?

Strength training can help slow bone loss and, in many cases, improve bone density. When muscles work against resistance, they pull on bones and signal the body to maintain or build stronger bone tissue. This type of effort is especially important for bone health. Additionally, high-intensity strength training encourages the release of chemical messengers in the body known as myokines that signal the creation of bone tissue.
Will lifting weights increase my risk of fractures?

Our Continuous Tension protocol and supervision ensure that the strength training is performed safely and avoids excessive or sudden loading during exercise. Properly performed strength training reduces fracture risk over time. Stronger muscles support and protect your bones, improve joint stability, and lower the risk of falls, which is the most common cause of fractures in people with low bone density.
What if I already have joint pain or past injuries?

Exercises are always adjusted to your comfort level and medical history. Machines, ranges of motion, and resistance levels are selected specifically to avoid painful or unsafe positions while still providing benefit.
Do I need to lift heavy weights for bone health?
You need enough resistance to challenge your muscles, but “heavy” is relative and always individualized. The goal is meaningful effort with precision control, not lifting maximal weights.
How long does it take to see benefits?

Improvements in strength, balance, and confidence often occur within a few sessions. Changes in bone density take longer to physiologically manifest and require consistency, but every workout contributes to protecting your long-term bone health.
Why not just do walking or light exercise?

Walking is excellent for overall health, but it does not provide enough stimulus to meaningfully strengthen bones. Strength training applies the kind of external resistance bones need to adapt and stay strong.
What makes MaxStrength Fitness different?
Our training focuses on slow, controlled movement, individualized resistance, and focused supervision. This allows us to safely work with clients who may not be comfortable with traditional gyms.

blocks.text: A framework for instructor exploration in finding the all important measure of a client's tolerance of effort.
1. What Are We Actually Trying to Achieve During the Workout?
Purpose of Resistance Training
Create a stimulus that produces strength, hypertrophy, and positive health adaptations.
The stimulus occurs when high mechanical tension is experienced by muscle fibers.
Mechanical tension is maximized when:
Effort is high
Motor unit recruitment is high
Contraction speed (i.e. movement arm) slows involuntarily
These happen closer to task failure
Lifting light weights for higher reps and creating a “burn” is not stimulative
Muscular Failure myth
“Muscular Failure” is not a structural phenomenon. Our muscles do not fail under load. This would only happen in an injurious scenario.
It is more accurately termed task failure — the point where the subject reaches their maximum tolerable perception of effort and decides to stop the task.
This point is highly individualized.

This point is also able to increase over time with practice. In other words, the best way to learn to tolerate training is by training; but it has to be intentional and not simply going through the motions!
2. What Does Appropriate Intensity Look Like (Eventually)?
A set is appropriately intense when:
The movement arm begins to involuntarily slow (“bogging down”).
The client must voluntarily increase effort to continue moving.
Concentric speed cannot be maintained without greater volitional effort. This increased effort creates higher levels of tension!
Quality (posture, pace, path, gradual load-up, continuous tension, controlled turnarounds) must be maintained.
Beginners/novice trainees may not need involuntary slowing for training to be productive. Quality execution should be the focus.
This combination ensures:
High motor unit recruitment (MUR)
High mechanical tension
Minimal unnecessary fatigue
Safety is the priority
3. The Instructor’s Role: Calibrating Intensity
Intensity is not forced — it is observed, discussed, and progressed.
A. Observational Cues
Monitor:
Facial expression (calm vs. strained)
Verbal feedback during set and in between
Breathing/oxygen debt
Body language (stillness vs. shifting)
Ability to maintain posture, pace, and path
B. Direct Communication
Ask early in a set (for a new/intensity adverse client):
“Does this weight feel reasonable?”
“Is this challenging in the way you expected?”
C. Instructor Responsibility
If effort is:
Too low - Increase load or reinforce qualitative execution.
Too high - Reduce load, reduce reps, or refine execution.
Misaligned with expectation - Discuss and recalibrate.
Always reassure:
Dialing in intensity is a skill that is individual specific and is critical to the development of a master level trainer. It is the instructor's responsibility!

If effort was perceived as too high, discuss with the subject and reassure them that we will adjust going forward. Empower them by reminding them that their effort is always under their control, we are simply facilitators. Unfortunately this is not an exact science and there is a learning curve for both but their safety is our highest priority.

If effort was perceived as too low, reassure the subject that they are still in the learning phase and that quality execution is the priority. We will also speed up the learning curve for them by adding more resistance to ensure an appropriate challenge going forward but quality comes first!

As noted above, in either case the instructor should determine the appropriateness of the load and make a change mid-set if deemed necessary. It is ultimately the instructor’s responsibility to deliver a remarkable client experience. Do not waste their time or money with anything less.
Both trainer and subject improve with practice.
4. Quality Before Intensity
Execution of the Continuous Tension protocol should be continually improved; rep to rep and workout to workout. The instructor must provide reminders and hold them accountable.
Controlled turnarounds are non-negotiable.
Gradual load-up for applicable exercises is equally important.
Less than “perfect” execution acts to artificially reduce perceived effort. It also unloads the targeted musculature.
If a set “felt easy,” evaluate:
Was the initial load up gradual?
Were turnarounds exaggerated and controlled?
Was pace/tension continuous?
Never sacrifice quality to just “keep the machine moving”.
5. Rep Range Framework
There is no single magic rep number.
The 6–10 range exists for structure and consistency of application.
General Guidelines
< 6 reps → Load may be too heavy. Can feel oppressive.
6–10 reps → Typically appropriate challenge.
> 10 reps → Load may be too light. Creates more discomfort.
~15 reps → Practical upper limit due to duration and focus.
Important Exceptions
Advanced subjects:
4–5 reps can be appropriate.
Heavier loads will produce strong stimulus sooner with less fatigue.
Newer but active subjects:
10–12 reps may accelerate learning through more “practice”.
If 15+ reps are possible with proper quality:
End the set.
Increase weight next session.
Emphasize the importance of every rep being “practice”.
Remember:
Lighter weights + higher reps = more discomfort/fatigue.
Fatigue is not the goal.
Mechanical tension from high effort is the goal.
6. Special Populations & Intensity Sensitivity
A. True Novices
Do not require maximal effort for stimulus.
Moderate load + skill acquisition can be sufficient.
Focus on control and learning the details (4 P’s).
B. Intensity-Adverse / Deconditioned
Easily overwhelmed.
Require lighter loads AND controlled rep counts.
Avoid excessive reps.
Keep upper limit ~15 reps (often fewer).
Build trust through careful progression.
Load alone does not usually cause the adverse response —
Total stress exposure does.
7. High-Drive/Experienced Clients
These clients:
Expect a challenge from day one.
Have higher tolerable perception of effort.
May disengage if under-challenged.
Instructor actions:
Avoid wasting time with light loads.
Assess load within first few reps.
Pause and increase weight if clearly too light.
Ensure sets approach meaningful (i.e. involuntary) slowing.
Give them:
Adequate challenge
Efficient stimulus
Instruction to maintain quality while increasing effort
8. When to Stop a Set
Stop when:
Ideally - Concentric failure (i.e. task failure) is reached with maintained quality. Basically, the loss of range of motion on the concentric.
Practically - Rep count reaches practical upper limit (~ 12-15).
Technique degrades.
Client is overwhelmed.
Safety is compromised.
You should:
Pause mid-set to adjust load.
End a set early to protect quality. If subject has clearly lost their form, they are no longer training, they are surviving.
Provide immediate corrective instruction. Even better would be to proactively provide instruction to prevent discrepancies.
9. Hierarchy of Priorities
Safety
Quality of execution
Appropriate effort (near task failure)
Established rep framework
The instructor is ultimately responsible for:
The safety of the client
The intensity of the session
The client’s experience
The effectiveness of the stimulus
10. How to End a Set Based on Subject and Exercise

Ideally, most clients will reach concentric failure somewhere between 6 and 10 reps, sometimes up to 12 if necessary. For the intensity adverse or deconditioned however, this may not be advisable as they tend to be more sensitive to loading and fatigue.
Most clients should reach concentric failure between 6–10 reps (occasionally up to 12).
Concentric failure = loss of full range of motion.
Only full reps are recorded; reps after this point are not counted for purposes of charting and progressing.
Partial Reps After Concentric Failure
Sets may continue past concentric failure using partial reps to increase muscular tension and stimulus.
This would only be for the clients that are deemed capable and tolerant of this level of increased intensity.
Most exercises lend themselves to partial reps, but the following do not:
Leg Press
Chest Press
Overhead Press
Seated Dip
Cervical
Lumbar
Partial reps (i.e. reps beyond concentric failure) are NOT advised for compound pushing movements (LP, CP, OH, SD):

Partial reps are often not possible once failure is reached due to inability to produce further concentric movement. The subject will most likely get “stuck” at the lower turn after reaching concentric failure on the preceding rep.
Partial reps (i.e. reps beyond concentric failure) are NOT advised for Cervical and Lumbar:
Safety concerns attributable to the delicate structures of the spine and nerves.
Concentric failure is also not recommended. Subjects should be capable of a full range of motion for all reps attempted.
Use an abundance of caution in both client selection and training intensity.
These two movements may not be advisable for all clients.
Considerations for Intensity-Adverse Clients
May not be appropriate for:
Concentric failure
Partial reps
Instructor must use judgment to avoid adverse responses.
As an alternative, consider an isometric intensifier to finish a set when concentric failure has not been reached.
Isometric Intensifier to End a Set (Primary Strategy for Intensity-Adverse Clients)
Purpose
Attempt to create meaningful effort and stimulus without requiring concentric failure.
General Application
Performed after the last full rep (before failure is reached).
Implemented at a specific point in the range of motion.
Typically lasts ~ 5 to 10 seconds with instructor-guided countdown and encouragement.
See next section below for specific application.
Isometric Intensifier - Application by Exercise Type
1. Compound Pushing Movements (LP, CP, OH, SD)
Perform isometric hold during the final eccentric phase.
Ideal position:
Near midpoint of range of motion
Slightly below midpoint (i.e. closer to lower turn) for increased intensity
Execution:
Client performs a slow “final descent”
Instructor cues a pause at a challenging but controllable position
Client works against the load to prevent movement
Safety feature:
Occurs during eccentric on the way to the lower turn where the load will be set down
Key Benefits
Increases effort without requiring failure
Client feels more capable and in control
Reduces likelihood of quitting early
2. All Other Movements (excluding Cervical/Lumbar)
Perform isometric hold at or near the contracted position.
Execution:
After last full concentric, hold the contracted position
Maintain tension with no movement
Instructor provides countdown and encouragement
Key Benefits
Occurs at a familiar and achievable position
Encourages engagement and effort
Clear “finish line” improves compliance
3. Cervical and Lumbar
Do NOT train to concentric failure.
Do NOT use partial reps.
Use only cautious isometric holds at the contracted position for appropriate subjects.
Coaching Component (Critical Across All Applications)
Instructor must:
Provide continuous encouragement
Count down remaining time (e.g., “5 more, 4 more…”)
Clients need:
A clear endpoint (“finish line”)
Ongoing verbal support to maintain effort
Key Takeaway

For intensity-adverse clients, isometric intensifiers are the most effective way to increase effort and stimulus while maintaining safety, confidence, and engagement—without requiring concentric failure.
Importantly, these isometric intensifiers are only used at the END of a set, never at random points prior to the end.
Important for New Instructors
Every client has a unique maximum tolerable perception of effort. Your job is to find it — safely and systematically.
A subject’s maximum tolerable perception of effort will improve with exposure to more training! This is the long-term “secret weapon”.
The instructor is responsible for ensuring that a stimulus has been created.
Most clients should eventually approach task failure in 6–10 reps. This can easily take months to arrive at.
Some never will — and that’s acceptable. We need to be creative and progress more slowly with these subjects.
Quality always precedes intensity.
Mechanical tension with high effort is the stimulus.
Fatigue, soreness, burning, sensations, etc. are NOT the objective and more importantly are NOT stimulative.

blocks.text: High-Intensity Resistance Training, as performed at MaxStrength Fitness, uses slow, controlled movements and instructor-guided effort to safely bring muscles to deep fatigue. This method delivers powerful, full-body benefits in minimal time.
1. Increased Strength
HIRT triggers the body to rebuild stronger by working muscles to true momentary fatigue. The MSF protocol makes strength improvements safe, efficient, and accessible for all fitness levels.
2. Improved Muscle Tone and Definition
Slow, controlled repetitions maximize muscle fiber recruitment, leading to greater firmness, shape, and overall muscle quality without risk from momentum.
3. Enhanced Metabolism
HIRT increases lean muscle tissue, elevating resting metabolic rate. Deep fatigue achieved in MSF sessions boosts post‑exercise calorie burn.
4. Time Efficiency
Just 20 minutes twice per week produces meaningful strength and health improvements. MSF delivers maximum return with minimal time commitment.
5. Increased Bone Density
High-intensity loading stimulates bone-building cells. MSF’s equipment and instruction allow clients to safely improve bone density without impact or risk.
6. Joint Health and Stability
Strengthening muscles and connective tissues improves joint support. The MSF method eliminates harmful forces, helping reduce discomfort and prevent injury.
7. Functional Strength for Daily Life
Clients gain strength that directly improves daily activities like lifting, climbing stairs, and maintaining mobility.
8. Cardiovascular Benefits
Working large muscle groups to deep fatigue elevates heart rate and challenges the cardiovascular system without traditional cardio or high impact.
9. Improved Blood Sugar Control
HIRT enhances insulin sensitivity and glucose metabolism, supporting clients concerned with energy levels, prediabetes, or Type 2 diabetes.
10. Reduced Injury Risk
MSF’s slow, controlled movements avoid momentum-based stress, making HIRT extremely safe for clients with past injuries or limitations.
11. Better Posture
Strengthening the core, back, and shoulder stabilizers improves alignment. Trainer cues at MSF reinforce strong, healthy posture.
12. Increased Mental Toughness
Training to high levels of effort builds confidence, discipline, and mental resilience. Clients often feel sharper and more capable.
13. Hormonal Benefits
HIRT naturally stimulates growth hormone and testosterone, supporting muscle building, fat loss, vitality, and recovery.
14. Improved Balance and Coordination
Strengthening stabilizing muscles enhances balance and neuromuscular control, especially important for aging clients.
15. Long-Term Health and Longevity
Resistance training is one of the strongest predictors of healthy aging, supporting metabolic health, mobility, and strength throughout life.
Myokines: The Hidden Health Advantage of High Intensity Resistance Training
When muscles work intensely, they release myokines — powerful chemical messengers that improve whole-body health. MSF’s deep-effort training style maximizes this response.
Key Myokine Benefits:
Reduced inflammation and decreased chronic pain
Enhanced fat metabolism, including conversion of white fat to brown fat
Better blood sugar control through improved insulin sensitivity
Brain health improvements (mood, memory, learning) via factors like BDNF
Stronger immune function and improved cellular repair
Longevity benefits driven by improved mitochondrial and metabolic function
Because MSF training uses controlled, full-body, high-intensity effort, clients experience some of the most potent myokine-driven benefits available in exercise.

topics.title: Training with pain (arthritis, fibro myalgia, tendonitis, bursitis, etc)
topics.source: docs/msf-academy/Academy 2/Training with pain (arthritis, fibro myalgia, tendonitis, bursitis, etc).txt

blocks.text: When working with clients who have chronic pain attributable to either genetic reasons or overuse injuries, the first step is always to ask whether they have been formally diagnosed and what limitations, if any, their physician has recommended. This applies to conditions such as arthritis, tendonitis including golfer’s or tennis elbow, carpal tunnel syndrome, and similar issues.

While we cannot reverse these conditions, we can often improve comfort and tolerance by strengthening the muscles and joints surrounding the affected area. Careful strength training increases the capacity of the tissues to handle load, which can reduce irritation during daily activities. This is an area where MaxStrength Fitness is uniquely effective, as our equipment allows us to train safely and precisely in ways that are often only available in a physical therapy setting.

Our main priority is always to assess tolerance. This means starting with very light resistance and possibly limiting the range of motion. If the client does not experience any increase in pain beyond what they normally feel, we can gradually add resistance and/or range of motion, and reassess. The goal is to find a level of load that is challenging but does not aggravate symptoms. Because our machines can be progressed in two pound increments, we can make very small, precise increases as the client adapts and gets stronger. The same can be done with the range of motion as well-small changes over time.

If the client is able to train with only limited use of the affected area, we may use most machines with either a static hold or timed static contraction (TSC) approach. As you’ll remember, a static hold involves holding an actual load in one position, usually near the midpoint in the range of motion. The TSC is a more conservative protocol where the subject will produce force against a static movement arm without holding a load. The movement arm is positioned in the desired location in the range of motion and then an excessive amount of weight is selected so that the movement arms cannot be moved. The subject is then instructed through three phases of increasing effort; 50%, 75%, and ending with an all out, 100% effort (or whatever can be comfortably sustained). Static execution allows us to strengthen the muscles around the joint without repeated movement that may irritate the area.

If the affected area happens to be the hands, wrists, or elbows and it is limiting to the point where we cannot train the upper body, we can work around it entirely while still delivering a productive workout. Hand pads are strongly recommended in these situations as they will blunt the pressure felt from the movement arm. If this is still too painful to endure, we may have to consider a “hands free” workout. With our full line of selectorized equipment, we can continue to train the major muscles of the shoulders and torso using machines such as the Lateral Raise, Simple Row, Pullover, and Chest Flye. All lower body and trunk machines remain fully available as well. This is an approach we have successfully used for many years.

The key point for clients to understand is that strength training does not have to worsen orthopedic conditions. When done carefully and intelligently, it can increase strength, improve joint support, and help clients feel more capable and confident in their daily lives. MaxStrength Fitness is well equipped to accommodate this and most other orthopedic concerns safely and effectively.
